titleText.es: Dentro de 60 millones de años, los extraterrestres conocerán a los humanos solo por un vídeo borroso de una mujer en un anuncio de Axe.
titleText.en: In sixty million years aliens will know humans only by a fuzzy clip of a woman in an Axe commercial.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official English title attributes are preserved exactly. OCR interleaved simultaneous panel text, omitted accents, fused true line wraps, misread CUANDO/EL/MUCHO, and produced one false flower-art token; the authored order follows the visible conversation. Ophrys apifera is audited as one excluded Latin scientific name with two physical boxes.

regions.labelEs: HAY UNAS ORQUÍDEAS CUYAS FLORES PARECEN ABEJAS HEMBRA.

applications.explanationEn: Cuyas agrees with the feminine plural possession flores and links it to the orchids.
Parecen directly introduces the noun comparison abejas hembra.

regions.labelEs: CUANDO LOS MACHOS INTENTAN APAREARSE CON ELLAS, TRANSFIEREN EL POLEN.

applications.explanationEn: Intentan carries the plural subject and present time; aparearse remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
Aparearse names mating and con introduces the other animals.

regions.labelEs: ESTAS ORQUÍDEAS (OPHRYS APIFERA) TIENEN FLORES, PERO NINGÚN MACHO SE POSA SOBRE ELLAS.

excludedUnits.rationale: Ophrys apifera is the unchanged Latin scientific name of the orchid species, not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

regions.labelEs: PORQUE LA ABEJA A LA QUE MIMETIZA SE EXTINGUIÓ HACE MUCHO.

applications.explanationEn: A marks the animate object, while la que refers back to the feminine singular bee.
The completed-past form presents the extinction as a bounded event.
Hace mucho places the event a long, unspecified time before the present.

regions.labelEs: SIN SUS COMPAÑERAS, ESTAS ORQUÍDEAS RECURREN A LA AUTOPOLINIZACIÓN, UNA ESTRATEGIA GENÉTICA DE ÚLTIMO RECURSO QUE SOLO RETRASA LO INEVITABLE.

applications.explanationEn: Recurren supplies the plural subject and a introduces the measure they turn to.
Genética follows estrategia and identifies the kind of strategy.
Genética takes the feminine singular form to agree with estrategia.
Último comes before recurso and uses its masculine singular ending to match that noun.
The established expression names the final option available.
Que introduces what the resource does; solo is an adverb inside the relative clause.
Neutral lo turns inevitable into an abstract idea: what is inevitable.

regions.labelEs: NADA QUEDA DE ESA ABEJA, PERO SABEMOS QUE EXISTIÓ POR LA FORMA DE LA FLOR.

applications.explanationEn: The completed-past form presents the bee's existence as belonging to a finished past period.

regions.labelEs: ES UNA IDEA DEL ASPECTO QUE TENÍA LA ABEJA HEMBRA A OJOS DE LA ABEJA MACHO...

applications.explanationEn: Que introduces the clause describing the appearance, and tenía supplies its past action.
The imperfect form describes the bee's appearance as an ongoing past state.
The fixed expression introduces the perspective from which the appearance is imagined.

regions.labelEs: ...EL ÚNICO RECUERDO DE LA ABEJA ES UNA PINTURA DIBUJADA POR UNA FLOR MORIBUNDA

applications.explanationEn: Único uses its masculine singular ending to agree with recuerdo.
Dibujada follows pintura and describes how the picture was made.
Dibujada is feminine singular to agree with pintura.
Moribunda follows flor and describes its condition.
Moribunda is feminine singular to agree with flor.

regions.labelEs: ORQUÍDEA, YO RECORDARÉ A TU ABEJA.

applications.explanationEn: The normally optional yo is printed to emphasize the speaker's personal promise.
Recordaré uses the simple-future ending for what the speaker promises to do.
Te marks the direct object beside the verb, and a ti repeats it in a stressed form for emphasis.
Recordaré states the speaker's future promise.

cards.noteEn: Orquídeas is the plural of orquídea.

example.en: The orchids bloom in spring.

cards.promptEs: orquídea · abeja extinta · pintura de una flor
cards.answerEn: an orchid preserving a vanished bee's appearance as a living memory
cards.noteEn: Some bee orchids evolved flowers that resemble female bees. The comic turns one self-pollinating orchid into a poignant memorial: even after the pollinating bee has disappeared, the flower's inherited shape still reflects how a plant once ‘saw’ that animal through evolution. Calling it a painting by a dying flower makes the biological relationship feel like art and remembrance.
Cuyas links a feminine plural possession to the person or thing mentioned before it. It agrees with the possessed noun, not the owner.

example.es: Conocí a una autora cuyas novelas admiro.
example.en: I met an author whose novels I admire.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish say ‘whose’ while matching the thing possessed?
cards.answerEn: Use cuyo, cuya, cuyos, or cuyas before the possessed noun; match that noun in gender and number.
cards.noteEn: The form agrees with what is possessed, not with the owner. Cuyas ideas means ‘whose ideas’ because ideas is feminine plural.

example.es: Conozco a un músico cuyas canciones son famosas.
example.en: I know a musician whose songs are famous.

cards.noteEn: Flores is the plural of flor.

example.en: The garden has yellow flowers.

cards.noteEn: Parecen is the plural present form of parecer. Before a noun it can describe resemblance, without saying that the things are literally identical.

example.en: Those clouds look like mountains.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something resembles or looks like a kind of thing?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of parecer followed directly by the comparison noun.
cards.noteEn: No como is required in this construction. Parece una nube means that something looks like a cloud; parecen nubes uses the plural verb and noun.

example.es: Desde lejos, las rocas parecen animales.
example.en: From far away, the rocks look like animals.

cards.noteEn: Abejas is the plural of abeja.

example.en: The bees visit the flowers.

cards.noteEn: For an animal, hembra identifies the female sex. It can follow the species noun and does not change for number in the same way as an ordinary adjective.

example.en: We saw two female wolves.

cards.noteEn: Machos is the plural noun for male animals.

example.en: The males have dark plumage.

cards.noteEn: Intentan is the present form of intentar for a plural subject.

example.en: They try to solve the problem.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: No linking preposition is needed between the two verbs. Intento abrir means “I try to open,” and intentamos salir means “we try to leave.” The attempted action stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: We try to open the window.

cards.noteEn: Aparearse is a pronominal verb used for animals mating. Its small pronoun changes with the subject.

example.en: The birds return to mate.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an animal mates with another animal?
cards.answerEn: Use aparearse con followed by the mate.
cards.noteEn: Aparearse is pronominal, so its small pronoun changes with the subject. Con introduces the other animal.

example.es: Estas aves se aparean con parejas de la misma especie.
example.en: These birds mate with partners of the same species.

cards.noteEn: Ellas is the feminine plural stressed pronoun. After a preposition it can mean ‘them.’

example.en: I spoke with them yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Transfieren is the plural present form of transferir.

example.en: The pipes transfer the heat.

cards.answerEn: no; not any (before a masculine singular noun)
cards.noteEn: Ningún is used directly before a masculine singular noun. When it comes after the verb, Spanish normally also keeps no before the verb: no tengo ningún problema.

example.en: We did not see any error.

cards.noteEn: As a noun for an animal, macho means a male.

example.en: No male came near.

cards.answerEn: the small pronoun used with posarse
cards.noteEn: Posarse is used when something lands or settles on a surface. The small pronoun changes with the subject: me poso, se posa, se posan.

example.es: La mariposa se posa en una hoja.
example.en: The butterfly lands on a leaf.

cards.noteEn: With se, posa is the singular present form of posarse, used when an animal or object comes to rest on a surface.

example.es: El pájaro se posa en la rama.
example.en: The bird lands on the branch.

cards.noteEn: Sobre can locate one thing above and supported by another. It has a separate common sense meaning ‘about.’

example.es: Las llaves están sobre la mesa.
example.en: The keys are on the table.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks an animate direct object
cards.noteEn: Spanish sometimes puts a before a direct object treated as animate or person-like. This can extend beyond people when animals, living things, or personified entities receive that treatment.

example.es: El cuento presenta a los árboles como personajes.
example.en: The story presents the trees as characters.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the feminine article in la que; helps mean which, who, or whom

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Mimetiza is the singular present form of mimetizar.

example.es: El insecto mimetiza una hoja seca.
example.en: The insect mimics a dry leaf.

cards.answerEn: the small pronoun used with extinguirse
cards.noteEn: Extinguirse describes a species, fire, or activity dying out. The small pronoun is part of this use.

example.es: La especie se extinguió hace siglos.
example.en: The species died out centuries ago.

cards.noteEn: With se, extinguió is a completed-past form of extinguirse for one species or thing.

example.es: Ese animal se extinguió hace mucho.
example.en: That animal became extinct long ago.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

example.en: I arrived two hours ago.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happened a long time ago?
cards.answerEn: Use hace mucho after the completed event.
cards.noteEn: Mucho supplies an unspecified long amount of elapsed time. For an exact duration, Spanish can instead use hace dos años or another stated period.

example.es: Ese tren dejó de funcionar hace mucho.
example.en: That train stopped operating long ago.

cards.noteEn: Mucho can stand by itself when the kind of amount is already clear. It then means ‘much’ or ‘a lot’ without a following noun.

example.en: —How much rice is left? —A lot.

cards.noteEn: Compañeras can mean companions or partners. For animals in a reproductive context, it can refer to mates.

example.es: Los pájaros buscan a sus compañeras.
example.en: The birds look for their mates.

cards.noteEn: Recurren is the plural present form of recurrir. With a it describes turning to a measure or solution.

example.es: A veces recurren a métodos antiguos.
example.en: Sometimes they resort to old methods.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone resorts or turns to a measure?
cards.answerEn: Use recurrir a followed by the measure, method, or person turned to.
cards.noteEn: The form of recurrir changes for the subject and time, but a remains before its complement.

example.es: El equipo recurrió a un plan alternativo.
example.en: The team resorted to an alternative plan.

cards.noteEn: Recurrir requires a before the measure, method, or person turned to.

example.en: She resorted to a temporary solution.

cards.noteEn: Autopolinización is pollination using pollen from the same flower or plant.

example.es: La planta puede reproducirse por autopolinización.
example.en: The plant can reproduce by self-pollination.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Genética is the feminine singular adjective related to genes or heredity.

example.en: They study genetic diversity.

cards.noteEn: Before a noun, último can mean the final or last remaining one, or simply the most recent one. The surrounding noun and situation distinguish those readings: el último superviviente is the last survivor, while mi último trabajo can mean my latest work.

example.en: I read his latest article.

cards.promptEs: número ordinal antes de un sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you use words such as first, second, or third before a Spanish noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the ordinal before the noun and make its ending match the noun's gender and number.
cards.noteEn: An ordinal gives a position in an order. Primero, segundo, tercero, último, and similar words usually come before the noun. Most forms use -o with a masculine singular noun and -a with a feminine singular noun, but primero and tercero shorten to primer and tercer before a masculine singular noun. Plural nouns use plural forms.

example.es: La segunda puerta está en el tercer piso.
example.en: The second door is on the third floor.

cards.questionEn: How do you name the final option used when other choices have failed?
cards.noteEn: Último comes before recurso because it ranks this option as the final one available.

example.es: La cirugía era el último recurso.
example.en: Surgery was the last resort.

cards.noteEn: Recurso can be something available for solving a problem, including a last resort.

example.es: La negociación fue nuestro último recurso.
example.en: Negotiation was our last resort.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Retrasa is the singular present form of retrasar.

example.en: The rain delays the departure.

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to “what is important,” “the difficult part,” or another general quality without naming a noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the unchanged word lo before a masculine-singular adjective: lo importante, lo difícil, lo bueno.
cards.noteEn: Here lo does not stand for a masculine object. It turns the quality into a general idea or aspect, such as lo importante, “what is important.” The adjective stays in its masculine singular form because there is no named noun for it to match.

example.en: The difficult part is starting.

cards.noteEn: Inevitable has the same form with masculine and feminine singular nouns.

example.en: The change seems inevitable.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

example.en: I don’t see anything.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Existió is a completed-past form of existir for one person or thing.

example.en: That bridge existed for centuries.

cards.noteEn: Por can introduce the evidence or clue that lets someone know or recognize something.

example.en: I recognized him from his voice.

cards.noteEn: Idea ends in -a but is a feminine noun: una idea.

example.en: I have an idea.

cards.noteEn: Del is the required contraction of de + el. It can mean “of the” or “from the,” depending on context.

example.en: I’m coming from the market.

cards.noteEn: Aspecto can describe what someone or something looks like.

example.es: El edificio tiene un aspecto antiguo.
example.en: The building has an old appearance.

cards.noteEn: Tenía is a past form of tener. It presents a state or characteristic that held at that past time without marking its beginning or end.

example.en: The house had a garden.

cards.answerEn: in; from (as part of a ojos de)
cards.noteEn: This a begins the fixed expression a ojos de, which introduces a person's or group's perspective.

example.es: A ojos del jurado, la prueba era clara.
example.en: In the jury's eyes, the evidence was clear.

cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘in the eyes of’ or ‘from the perspective of’?
cards.answerEn: Use a ojos de before the person or group whose perspective is meant.
cards.noteEn: The expression is often figurative: a ojos del público means ‘in the public's eyes.’

example.es: A ojos de sus vecinos, era una heroína.
example.en: In the eyes of her neighbors, she was a heroine.

cards.noteEn: Interpretada is the feminine singular completed-action form of interpretar.

example.es: La señal fue interpretada por el equipo.
example.en: The signal was interpreted by the team.

cards.noteEn: This is the living-organism sense of planta, not a floor of a building or an industrial facility.

example.en: The plant needs light.

cards.noteEn: Used on its own as an exclamation, vaya can express surprise, admiration, or annoyance. This conversational use is distinct from vaya as a form of the verb ir, 'to go.'

example.en: Wow, what a surprise!

cards.noteEn: Único changes to única, únicos, or únicas to match the person or thing it describes.

example.en: It is the only open road.

cards.noteEn: This sense names an artistic picture made with paint, not the paint material itself.

example.es: El museo compró una pintura antigua.
example.en: The museum bought an old painting.

cards.noteEn: Dibujada is the feminine singular completed-action form of dibujar used as a description.

example.es: Vimos una figura dibujada a mano.
example.en: We saw a figure drawn by hand.

cards.noteEn: Moribunda is the feminine singular form used for a living being near death.

example.en: They tried to save the dying plant.

cards.questionEn: Why might Spanish say tú or yo when the verb already tells you who acts?
cards.answerEn: Say the subject pronoun to add emphasis, contrast, or clarity; otherwise Spanish often leaves it out.
cards.noteEn: A verb form such as eres already points to “you.” Adding tú can stress that particular person, especially in a contrast or a surprised question. The pronoun may appear after the verb.

example.en: I didn't go; you did.

cards.noteEn: Recordaré is the simple future form of recordar for yo.

example.en: I will remember your advice.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: Why can Spanish mark who or what is directly affected by an action with a short word and then emphasize that same target again after a?
cards.answerEn: Put the short object word with the verb. To clarify or contrast the same target, add a stressed form beginning with a, such as a mí or a todos.
cards.noteEn: Me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, and las can identify who or what the verb acts on. Spanish can repeat that target with an emphasized clarifier beginning with a, especially a stressed form such as a mí, a ti, or a todos. With an unchanged dictionary-form verb, the short marker attaches to the end, as in invitarnos or verlos. In the prompt, the slashes list alternatives, each plus sign means “followed by,” and the dots mean that other words may appear between the verb and its clarifier.

example.en: They invited all of us.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces an emphasized object such as a mí
cards.noteEn: A stressed form such as a mí can repeat a short object pronoun such as me for contrast or emphasis. English normally expresses the emphasis through stress rather than an extra word.

example.en: You cannot see me in particular.
